name: Myo-reps / drop sets

lead: Drop sets and myo-reps are intensity techniques that pack more hard repetitions into less time so you get more muscle-building work per minute. A drop set keeps going with a lighter weight after failure at a heavier one; myo-reps use one high-effort set followed by several short mini-sets with brief rests.

Both keep the muscle working near failure for more total reps in a short window, which advocates say raises the growth stimulus per minute. Drop sets have a long history: Henry Atkins described the multi-poundage system in the late 1940s and they were part of Joe Weider's system in the 1980s. Coverage says drop sets may increase muscle growth more than traditional three-set training, while some researchers report mixed findings; a 2026 trial compared myo-reps with straight sets in resistance-trained men.

paras: Lifters tack them on to the last set of an exercise or use them for isolation moves when time is short. They are used inside a normal split alongside heavier compound work.
Working to failure adds fatigue and soreness, and general resistance-training injury risks apply. No technique-specific harm data were identified.

chain: Extra hard reps in less time
angle.text: Lifters use drop sets and myo-reps to pack more hard reps into less time, so shorter workouts still give a strong growth stimulus. Drop sets go back to the 1940s and may add growth compared with traditional sets, with some mixed findings. Myo-reps were only recently compared with straight sets in a trial.

lead: Drop sets and myo-reps are resistance-training intensity techniques meant to pack more hard repetitions into less time, which lifters use to build muscle size more efficiently. A drop set continues exercising with a lighter weight immediately after reaching muscle failure at a heavier one.  Myo-reps are a related method in which a lifter performs one high-effort activation set and then several short mini-sets with brief rests. [1][2]

Drop sets have a long documented history: Henry Atkins, editor of Body Culture magazine, described the approach in the late 1940s as the "multi-poundage system", and drop sets were part of Joe Weider's Weider System in the 1980s.  Myo-reps are newer; a T Nation post credits Borge Fagerli with creating them as a type of rest-pause training. [2]

For physique-building, the appeal is more working sets near failure in a short session, which proponents say raises the muscle-growth stimulus per minute. A systematic review of drop sets found six studies with 142 participants, [3] and a 2026 meta-analysis of advanced training systems reported a small, significant pooled advantage over traditional training, driven mainly by strength outcomes. [4] A 2026 trial compared myo-reps with straight sets in resistance-trained men. [5]

paras: Drop sets are most often done on weight machines but can also use dumbbells and other free weights.  Variations include fixed-rep steps, wide drops (30% or more per step) versus tight drops (roughly 10-25%), and "down sets" with rest between weights.

Myo-reps pair an activation set, described on T Nation as roughly 9 to 25 or more reps, with up to several mini-sets of 3-5 reps separated by short rests. [2] The method is classed as a rest-pause variant and promoted as a time-efficient alternative to several straight sets. [2][1]

A narrative review of time-efficient training concluded that advanced techniques such as supersets, drop sets and rest-pause training can roughly halve session time compared with traditional training while maintaining training outcomes. [6] A systematic review of advanced techniques found drop and cluster sets may provide an additional stimulus relative to traditional training. [7]

Encyclopedic coverage says drop sets may increase muscle growth more than traditional three-set training and cites a 12-week study of adults in their 50s who improved muscle mass, strength, endurance and functional tasks, while noting that some researchers report mixed or inconclusive results.

A 2026 meta-analysis of 23 studies in recreationally trained adults reported a small, statistically significant overall advantage for advanced systems (g = 0.159), a moderate benefit for strength (g = 0.351) and a small, non-significant effect for hypertrophy (g = 0.046). [4] A 2026 narrative review of 40 recent studies reported that several found no between-method differences, though small samples preclude conclusions of equivalence. [8]
Working to failure adds fatigue and soreness, and the general injury risks of resistance training apply. No technique-specific harm data were located.

sections.h: Use in looksmaxxing and physique communities
paras: On T Nation, myo-reps appear regularly in training logs, for example on cable raises, tricep extensions, hammer curls and incline presses, [9][10][11] and one lifter noted that a 12-minute window left room for myo-reps. [12] Lifters also mention drop sets among a long list of intensity techniques for the concentric phase. [13]

A systematic review and meta-analysis of drop sets for hypertrophy included six studies and 142 participants aged 19-27. [3] A systematic review of advanced techniques included 30 articles. [7] A 2015 randomised trial in 14 male strength-trained athletes compared five lower-limb training protocols, including drop sets, using tensiomyography to assess neuromuscular function. [14]

A 2026 randomised comparison of rest-pause versus drop-set progressive overload assessed body composition and strength in 23 resistance-trained adults. [15] A 2026 study compared myo-reps and straight sets in resistance-trained men for strength, hypertrophy and time. [5] A registered trial (n=34) compares myo-reps with traditional sets for strength, fat-free mass and time efficiency. [5] A 2025 study found cluster sets and traditional sets produced similar hypertrophy when volume and effort were matched. [16]

lore.intro: Lifters on T Nation use myo-reps and drop sets as finishing techniques and time savers, and share them in training logs. [2][9][12]
